title: Luxury as Enemy of Love
author: John Mark Reynolds
source: johnmarkreynolds.substack.com (Canon: John Mark N. Reynolds), October 4, 2026
summary: Reynolds reads Plato's Phaedrus as a lesson on why luxury is the enemy of love and of wisdom. Phaedrus arrives from a day of indulgent talk at the house of Lysias, still captivated by a speech that is full of high-sounding words but empty of meaning. Socrates walks him out of the city to a plane tree and, through simple nature, old stories and honest discussion, frees him from that spell. Reynolds defines luxury as spending the time hard work has bought on useless entertainment, and he argues that the very wealth that makes leisure for philosophy possible also tempts us away from it. He applies the point to a culture of easy video entertainment, phones designed to sell amusement to children, and universities that chase clicks over truth. The remedy he offers is modest and physical: gardens, trees, fasting, real conversation, and the posture of a lover of wisdom rather than a dilettante.
points: Reynolds argues that luxury is not a moral problem only because of waste but because it produces boredom and dulls our awareness of ideas and spiritual things.
The Phaedrus scene is read as a contrast between two kinds of speech, the fat but meaningless speech of Lysias and the love of the Good that Socrates models.
Socrates loves Phaedrus as a fellow seeker rather than as a prize, which marks the difference between love and desire.
The author insists the problem is not civilization itself, since leisure for discussion is a product of a sophisticated society, but the temptation that wealth brings with it.
His practical cure is simple: nature, fasting, good talk, and refusing to treat wisdom as something one can hook up with casually.
quotes: Luxury is fun on a holiday, but it can be deadly in a lifetime, keeping us from knowing true love. Fasting sharpens our awareness of ideas and spiritual things.
Successful people I have known often live relatively simple personal lives. They know that eating holiday food every day leaves nothing for a feast.

Socrates loves Phaedrus not as a prize, an object, but as a fellow human being in search of love. Socrates wishes what is best for Phaedrus and himself, while understanding that the easiest mistake is to confuse desire with love.

The problem is not civilization. Having the time for a discussion is the product of a sophisticated society. The danger is that the very wealth that can buy time for the pursuit of God and wisdom tempts us to luxury.
Luxury is using the time hard work has given us on useless entertainment and endless fripperies.
Love is missing in the speech of Lysias that Phaedrus thinks so beautiful. It is fat with words, but short on meaning. That is the nature of luxury: stuff without purpose, wasteful.
Our children are, God save them, given mobile devices psychologically designed to sell entertainment.
We must refuse the role of dilettante for that of the lover. We cannot hook up with wisdom. She refuses her consent to anyone who will not commit for eternity.
